lead: Requirements elicitation is planned conversation with every person who affects or is affected by a system. It exists because no single manager knows how booking clerks handle a refund at 11 p.m., what a regulator checks, or where a passenger gives up. You identify stakeholders, map their interest and influence, and gather views in interviews, workshops, observation and prototypes. The output is a shared, recorded understanding, not a wish list. Some syllabi call this requirements gathering; 'capture' is misleading because users cannot hand over complete requirements.
prereq: You need: the process loop and feasibility check in Chapter 2.2, plus the split between functional and non-functional requirements in Chapter 2.1.

blocks.text: A stakeholder is any person or group who affects the system or is affected by it. For a rail booking system, passengers buy tickets, booking clerks handle changes, finance officers reconcile money, IT operations keep the service running, and a regulator sets rules. Support staff, trainers, accessibility representatives and maintainers also matter. Missing an operator is a common failure: the software works in the demo but fails at the counter. Primary stakeholders use the system; secondary stakeholders support it; external stakeholders regulate or depend on it.

Build a stakeholder map. Interest is how much the outcome matters to the stakeholder. Influence is the power to change, fund, block or regulate the system. Place each name on the map. High-influence stakeholders need early engagement. High-interest stakeholders need frequent communication. A person can be high on both. For each stakeholder, record role, goal, interest level, influence level, contact, and what they can tell you. Use the map to plan who comes to which workshop, not to rank human worth. A regulator with low daily interest but high influence can still stop a release. An accessibility representative may have low formal power but high interest and legal weight.

Collaborative gathering means users, operators and analysts build the requirement together. The analyst does not arrive with a finished form. Use more than one method because each sees a different part of the work. An interview is a planned one-to-one conversation. Ask open questions, then ask for a recent real case. A workshop puts different stakeholders in one room. It is fast for exposing conflict, but needs an agenda, a facilitator and a written record.

A focus group is a discussion with similar users, such as six booking clerks. It shows shared norms, but can hide individual exceptions. A questionnaire reaches many people cheaply. Use closed answers for counts and a few open answers for reasons. Observation means watching work at the counter or on a phone. It reveals steps people forget to mention, such as checking a paper register before overriding a fare. Document analysis reads forms, refund rules, audit reports and complaint logs. Brainstorming generates many ideas before judging them. A prototype is a cheap mock screen or paper form; people react to what they can see. Choose methods by risk: observation for messy operator work, workshops for conflicting goals, questionnaires for wide user groups, prototypes when the interface is uncertain. No method proves completeness; combine them and check back.

sections.h3: First questions, workshop and work products

blocks.text: Start with three first questions. Who books, changes or cancels? What fails today? What must never happen? Ask for a recent example, the workaround used, and who pays when it fails. Write the speaker's role beside every answer. A passenger and a finance officer mean different things by 'safe'.

Use a timed agenda. For 12 people in 90 minutes: welcome and rules 10 min; first questions 20 min; conflict listing 30 min; resolution by ranking 20 min; recap and owners 10 min. Invite 4 passengers, 3 booking clerks, 2 finance officers, 2 IT operations staff and 1 accessibility representative. Put must-never items first. List conflicts in a visible table: issue, who wants what, why. Resolve by ranking, not by averaging. Mandatory rules come first; convenience features become later options. In the rail example, passengers want one-click booking, while finance wants OTP and an audit trail. Audit trail is mandatory; one-click becomes a remembered passenger profile after authentication. Record decision, owner and date, then pass it to validation and management.

Work products: stakeholder register, map, interview notes, workshop minutes, conflict log, question list, observation notes, document extracts, prototype feedback and first usage scenarios. Keep raw notes and a one-page summary. A scenario is one path through a task; write the main path and failure paths. Use case writing belongs to 2.6; SRS wording to 2.5. Call it elicitation, not capture. Capture suggests users can hand over complete requirements. In reality people know routines, not missing rules; stakeholders contradict each other; and new software changes the work. Elicitation is joint discovery: ask, observe, model, check back.

spec.aria: A 90-minute timeline: welcome 10, first questions 20, conflict listing 30, resolution 20 and recap 10, with the middle three bracketed as 70 minutes of elicitation. Below, five boxes of 4 minutes each and a row of 12 participant dots.

examples.question: An IRCTC-style rail booking team runs a 90-minute elicitation workshop with 12 participants: 4 passengers, 3 booking clerks, 2 finance officers, 2 IT operations staff and 1 accessibility representative. The agenda is: welcome 10 min, first questions 20 min, conflict listing 30 min, conflict resolution 20 min, recap 10 min. (a) Find total participant-minutes. (b) Find the percentage of workshop time used for elicitation, where elicitation is first questions plus conflict listing plus conflict resolution. (c) If the 20-minute conflict-resolution block is split equally across the five stakeholder groups, how many minutes does each group get? Give units.
steps: Total participant-minutes = number of participants × minutes per participant = 12 × 90 = 1080 participant-minutes.
Elicitation time = first questions + conflict listing + conflict resolution = 20 + 30 + 20 = 70 minutes.
Five stakeholder groups are passengers, booking clerks, finance, IT operations and accessibility. Minutes per group = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 minutes.
examples.answer: Total participant-minutes = 1080 participant-minutes; elicitation percentage = 77.78%; conflict-resolution time per stakeholder group = 4 minutes.

participants = 12
minutes = 90
total = participants * minutes
elicit = 20 + 30 + 20
percent = round(100 * elicit / minutes, 2)
per_group = 20 / 5
print(total)

print(per_group)

traps: Listing only the paying customer. Operators, support staff, regulators and maintainers can block or break the system.
Treating 'requirements capture' as handover. Users cannot give complete requirements; ask, observe and check back.
Confusing interest with influence. A regulator may care little daily but can stop a release; a passenger may care deeply but cannot fund it.
Running a workshop without a timed agenda and conflict log. The loudest person wins and decisions disappear.
Interviewing only managers. The counter clerk knows the workaround that the manager's process diagram omits.

quiz.a: Any person or group who affects the system or is affected by it.

quiz.q: Why is 'requirements capture' a misleading name?
quiz.a: It suggests users can hand over complete requirements; in fact requirements are discovered through conversation, observation and checking.

quiz.q: A 60-minute workshop has 10 participants. Compute total participant-minutes.
Passengers want one-click booking; finance wants OTP and an audit trail. How do you resolve this?
quiz.a: Rank mandatory rules first. Keep audit trail and OTP as mandatory; turn one-click into a remembered profile after authentication.

quiz.q: In a 90-minute agenda, elicitation blocks are 20, 30 and 20 minutes. What percentage of the workshop is elicitation? Give one decimal place.
When is observation better than a questionnaire?
quiz.a: When work has tacit steps or workarounds that people forget to report; observation shows the real sequence.

quiz.q: You have a high-influence regulator and high-interest passengers. How does the stakeholder map change engagement?
quiz.a: Engage the regulator early for rules and sign-off; communicate frequently with passengers for needs and feedback. Do not use one meeting for both purposes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry product teams use continuous discovery: short interviews every week, a living stakeholder map, and requirement mining from support tickets and app reviews. Participatory design brings users into prototyping. Research search terms: stakeholder salience, requirements workshop facilitation, apprenticeship observation, participatory design. Newer curricula may call this product discovery or needs analysis.
